#2080. West Ham Go Full Circle as Blackburn Expose Familiar Problems

West Ham’s 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers was a particularly frustrating result because, for large periods of the game, Scott Parker’s side appeared to be the better team. We started brightly, enjoyed plenty of possession and created opportunities, yet somehow managed to leave Ewood Park with nothing.

What concerns me most isn’t necessarily the result itself, although that’s bad enough. It’s the manner in which West Ham gradually deteriorated as the afternoon progressed. Even after Joël Piroe pulled a goal back late on, I thought we looked increasingly disorganised and short of confidence.

And that’s perhaps the strangest aspect of Parker’s first two matches. We started against Cardiff looking completely devoid of confidence, rediscovered it during that extraordinary second-half comeback, began confidently against Blackburn and somehow finished looking just as nervous as we had before.

I was actually quite encouraged by the opening stages. West Ham pressed high, moved the ball around reasonably well and looked determined to take the game to Blackburn. Max Kilman was particularly proactive, stepping out of defence to offer an additional passing option, while Divine Mukasa and Arne Engels were regularly involved in midfield.

Down the left, Ezra Mayers and Edvin Austbø developed a promising partnership. Mayers was willing to get forward and Austbø looked lively, producing one lovely piece of skill to beat two Blackburn players before delivering a dangerous cross.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

However, there was a problem developing on that side of the pitch. Blackburn repeatedly managed to isolate Mayers against two opponents, and while the youngster was doing some good things offensively, he wasn’t receiving enough protection defensively.

Joël Piroe was also struggling to make the most of promising situations. On one occasion, he found himself with only a single defender to beat but hesitated for so long that three opponents eventually surrounded him. West Ham were having plenty of the ball, but Blackburn were defending deeply and making it difficult to create clear opportunities.

The second half initially offered more encouragement. Mavropanos headed narrowly wide from an Engels corner, Piroe had an effort saved and then Austbø produced an excellent cross which Bowen headed against the post. At that stage, West Ham were piling on the pressure and Blackburn were struggling to get out of their own half.

Then came the sucker punch. In the 54th minute, Blackburn broke down their right, with Mayers unable to stop the delivery into the penalty area. Andri Guðjohnsen converted, but I thought several West Ham players could have done better.

Austbø might have provided more protection for Mayers, Mavropanos could have defended the situation better and I certainly felt Mads Hermansen should have been more commanding. Whether he caught the cross, punched it or simply got something on the ball, I thought the goalkeeper had an opportunity to intervene.

It was a horrible goal to concede, particularly given how much of the attacking West Ham had been doing. Parker responded by introducing Manor Solomon for Austbø, a substitution I found surprising. The Norwegian had been one of our more involved attacking players, while Solomon subsequently struggled to make any impression.

Mohamadou Kanté was then replaced by Taty Castellanos, but West Ham were finding it increasingly difficult to establish the same attacking rhythm. Blackburn’s second goal arrived in the 71st minute, with Afolayan producing an excellent finish.

Kilman had gone down following contact to his face, but too many West Ham players appeared more interested in appealing for a foul than dealing with the danger. Engels, in particular, could have done more to close down the shot. Whatever the circumstances, you cannot simply stop defending because you believe the referee should have awarded a free kick.

At 2-0, the game appeared to be slipping away, but West Ham eventually found a route back through something remarkably straightforward. Castellanos got down the right-hand side and delivered a dangerous ball into the penalty area. Piroe reacted quickly and fired high into the roof of the net in the 82nd minute.

It was an excellent finish from a striker who, in truth, hadn’t been having a particularly good afternoon. But sometimes football really is that simple. Get the ball wide, get down the line and deliver something dangerous into the box. Give your centre-forward an opportunity to attack the ball.

Suddenly it was Blackburn 2-1 West Ham, with enough time remaining to rescue a point. Unfortunately, the expected late onslaught never really materialised. In fact, I thought West Ham became progressively worse.

Mavropanos endured a dreadful few minutes, fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping and gifting Blackburn a counter-attack. He then slipped again while attempting to recover, while Souček subsequently played a very poor pass into Lewis Orford inside our own penalty area, creating another potentially disastrous situation.

West Ham looked increasingly nervous, and the defensive organisation seemed to disappear. There were still opportunities at both ends in stoppage time, with Todd Cantwell shooting straight at Hermansen when Blackburn might have made it 3-1.

Souček then headed directly at the Blackburn goalkeeper following an excellent chipped delivery from Bowen. It was precisely the sort of position from which we’ve seen Souček score numerous times, but once again West Ham had failed to make the most of a promising opportunity.

I keep coming back to the confidence issue because I think it explains an awful lot about what we’ve witnessed over these two matches. Against Cardiff, West Ham were absolutely dreadful during the opening 45 minutes, before producing a transformation after half-time that was almost impossible to believe.

Suddenly the players looked confident, aggressive and capable of playing some very good football. That improvement appeared to carry into the opening stages at Ewood Park, where we pressed Blackburn, moved the ball with purpose and looked considerably more comfortable in possession.

Yet by the closing stages, the confidence had completely evaporated. It was almost as though we’d gone full circle in the space of two matches, ending up precisely where we started. That is particularly disappointing because I still believe this West Ham squad possesses considerably more ability than recent performances suggest.

There were some positives. Mukasa showed invention, Austbø looked dangerous, Kilman had a decent game and Piroe took his goal extremely well. But the defensive mistakes, poor decision-making and increasingly nervous football were all too familiar.

I don’t think Scott Parker can be held responsible for everything we’ve witnessed this week. He’s barely had any meaningful time on the training pitch, and the international break offers him an opportunity to start properly implementing his ideas.

However, the evidence of these two games suggests that restoring confidence isn’t simply a matter of delivering one rousing team talk. The psychological side of West Ham’s problems may be every bit as important as the tactical side.

The frustrating thing is that we’ve already seen how much better these players can perform when they believe in themselves. Against Blackburn, we watched that belief gradually disappear again.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

#2079. Everton dispatch Newcastle to give Matthias Jaissle a reality check

Everton appear well ahead of Newcastle United in their preparation for the new Premier League season after a comfortable 3-1 victory at Murrayfield.

On a sobering evening for new Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle, who changed all 10 outfield players at half-time, Everton’s one and two-touch attacking play proved difficult to contain.

Everton took the lead through Thierno Barry after a defensive error from Sven Botman, before Iliman Ndiaye scored a penalty that was won cheaply by summer signing Hayden Hackney.

Newcastle’s raft of half-time changes helped David Moyes’s team strengthen their grip further, with Tyrique George adding a stylish third and 19-year-old Harrison Armstrong providing his second assist of the game.

Among the Newcastle players introduced at half-time was 18-year-old Sean Steur, the exciting midfield prospect signed from Ajax this summer. Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Toure also flickered with promise, but a sharp start from Jaissle’s team faded.

They pulled a goal back late on when Jacob Murphy’s cross found Harvey Barnes at the back post, but they offered little as an attacking force throughout the second half.

Newcastle have two more friendlies, against Bayer Leverkusen and Strasbourg, before they begin their Premier League season at home to Liverpool.

The club are reeling from the summer departures of Bruno Guimaraes, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and manager Eddie Howe, but David Hopkinson, the chief executive, struck a bullish tone when he spoke of this being the start of “Newcastle 2.0”.

Everton look the more settled side and club, and the performances of new arrivals Hackney and George were encouraging, while Thierno Barry was sharp in the centre-forward position that has proved so difficult for the club to fill in recent seasons.

Everton kick-off their new season at home to Crystal Palace, and keeping Ndiaye at the club beyond the end of the transfer window will be a priority.

The scoreline is a fair reflection of the game. Everton looked sharper, as well as fitter, and there are more positives for them to take. They look ready for the new season, Newcastle need reinforcements.

Alcaraz bends a shot not far wide from 25 yards for Everton. The game is meandering towards its conclusion now.

Willock collects the ball between the lines, feeds Murphy wide right, and his ball across goal is turned in at the back post by Harvey Barnes.

Moyes makes another pair of changes: Keane and Hackney off, O’Brien and Foster on.

Everton fans are enjoying themselves now, belting out Spirit of the Blues at Murrayfield.

More defending for Newcastle to do but they deal with Hackney’s corner delivery. All too easy for Everton to slice through their midfield in the build up though.

That goal had been coming, and Tyrique George is heavily involved again. He carries the ball forward and finds Armstrong, who returns the favour. George shoots on the swivel and picks out the bottom corner.

If I were a Newcastle fan in the stands, Edinbugh’s city centre hostelries would be looking very alluring just about now. There is not much for them to watch in this season half, they are chasing shadows. Some of that can be put down to the handful of young plyers in their second-half XI.

Tyler Dribbling drops a shoulder down the right, and wins a corner off Harvey Barnes. Everton are finishing this game the stronger, there are more goals in this should they put their foot on the pedal.

Newcastle, with some youngsters in their defence, looking a little ragged against Everton’s direct attacks now, but George runs into traffic at the edge of the box. Then Alcaraz is booked for a cynical foul.

Three more Everton changes on the way: Beto, Dibling and Alcaraz on for Barry, Ndiaye and Dewsbury-Hall.

Hayden Hackney plays a one-two with Tyrique George for Everton, with the former Chelsea winger backheeling the ball into Hackney’s path, and there were unheeded calls for a penalty. It was more of a penalty than the one Everton were awarded in the first half, Lewis Miley tripped him.

Thierno Barry’s performance has been a positive for Everton, could he nail down the No 9 role this season? It has been a problem position for several seasons now. Barry is tripped and Everton have a free-kick.

Dewsbury-Hall almost sneaks a shot in at the near post, but Hornicek tips the ball around the post.

Joe Willock with what was very nearly an exquisite disguised pass, but the flag was up for offside against Jacob Murphy.

Then an amusing moment: great cheers from the crowd as David Moyes heads a Hornicek clearance back down the line. He didn’t fancy the cushioned first touch off his instep, then.

Everton have played some quick one and two-touch football around the box in this game, and another move ends with George shooting over the bar. Everton are making their first change: Patterson off, replaced by Rohl.

The game is still finding its shape again after all those Newcastle changes, but Murphy did force a sharp save from Travers with a low shot from a tight angle.

He keeps to his word from before the game; Hornicek is the only player still on the pitch.

The players on for Newcastle are: Woltemade, Murphy, Willock, Barnes, Ramsey, Johnson, Steur, Pivas, Miley and Charlton.

It looks like an unchanged team from David Moyes, so Everton have a significantly more mature team on the pitch now.

Newcastle made a bright start, but as the half progressed there is no doubt that Everton have been the more dangerous attacking force and the scoreline reflects that. Here come the changes...

Everton have a late corner to defend, after another burst forward from Newcastle’s left-winger Toure. Newcastle try one off the training ground but the ball is cleared.

Thierno Barry almost finds the run of Hackney into the Newcastle penalty, and after a sluggish start, Everton have played some slick football in the attacking third.

A sign of some Newcastle frustration there was Wissa kicks Tyrique George across the shins. A bit naughty that, may even have been worthy of VAR attention in a Premier League game.

The Senegalese sends Hornicek the wrong way and finds the corner. No chance it was a penalty in the first place though, thankfully this is not a competitive game.

This is very soft, there was not much of a challenge by Joelinton on Dewsbury-Hall, but the Everton midfielder goes down in the box and is awarded the penalty.

It really should be 2-0 to Everton, a high-class moving down their left with Armstrong dinking a pass to Barry. He squared to Ndiaye who was free as a bird in the middle, but his shot was too close to Hornicek.

Joelinton runs down a blind alley before lumping a pass out for an Everton throw, and then the Newcastle man fouls Barry. The big Brazilian still finding his legs and getting up to speed.

A moment to forget for both Newcastle centre-backs. Thiaw was bumped and unbalance by Barry, before Botman steps out of defence and kicks fresh air against the Everton forward. Great recovery from Lewis Hall, but the ball breaks for Armstrong, who feeds Barry and he finishes across Hornicek.

Ndiaye has had a quiet start to the game for Everton, but his jinking qualities were on display there to beat a couple of Newcastle defenders. Everton lose the ball in midfield, and Tarkowski makes a superb last-ditch tackle to deny Osula.

Half-hearted appeals for a penalty from Wissa, but Hayden Hackney did not do much wrong. Looks like we will be spared a first-half hydration break, despite it being a sultry evening.

Osula skips through a couple of challenges at the edge of the area but fails to pick a pass in the box. Bazoumana Touré has looked lively for Newcastle on their left flank, and Bamba has done well for them in midfield.

Everton shake themselves into life as an attacking force. Cracking cross from Patterson into the box and Dewsbury-Hall’s run had gone untracked, but he was just stretching and could not generate enough power to beat Hornicek.

Good save from Travers to deny Elanga, but it was Mykolenko who made a hash of things in the box. The left back simply fell over the ball under no pressure. Newcastle the sharper of the two teams so far.

Joelinton feeds Bamba down the left wing for Newcastle who delivers a cross into the penalty area. Keane can only direct his defensive header back towards the penalty spot, but Wissa volleyed over with a first-time hit. Decent chance.

Thierno Barry makes it stick and proves a strong outlet for Everton. Botman brings him down at the expense of a free-kick just beyond the halfway line. Then Wissa drives into the penalty area for Newcastle after a one-two but he fouls Patterson.

Newcastle, playing in their lilac away kit, are the team trying to take the initiative with the ball, but Everton are quite happy staying compact and absorbing pressure. Elanga’s corner delivery is promising, but Osula does not connect cleanly at the back post.

Newcastle’s defenders enjoying comfortable possession in the early stages, Everton sitting off in their 4-4-2 defensive shape.

Wissa peels behind Everton’s defence inside the opening 90 seconds but he cannot lift the ball over Travers.

Bagpipes greet the players at Murrayfield, where the pitch has been reconfigured for football. There are only fans in the lower tier, and still plenty of empty seats even so.

We know it is a time in the pre-season when the legs are not that fresh, we train very intense but we want to play with an idea of how we want to play football. Intense with a vertical approach for sure, everyone gets 45 minutes except the goalkeeper.

Big Dunc and Moyes catch up pre-match! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/Jh4APHOZvX

A word that keeps being used about Jaissle is “special”. Newcastle’s hierarchy believe they have secured the services of a manager who will soon be recognised in the elite tier of European managers. We shall see how this view of the 38-year-old survives contact with a brutal and relentless Premier League campaign.

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; Shahar, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; Joelinton, Bamba; Elanga, Wissa, Toure; Osula

Newcastle subs: Gillespie, Harris, Charlton, Pivas, Johnson, M Miley, Finneran, Ramsey, Steur, Willock, J Murphy, Barnes, Neave, Woltemade

Your Mags at Murrayfield! ✊ pic.twitter.com/rDXpn0MqCg

Everton XI: Travers; Patterson, Tarkowski, Keane, Mykolenko; Hackney, Deswbury-Hall, Armstrong, Ndiaye; George, Barry

Here's how we start against Newcastle. UTT! 🔵📺 https://t.co/2VsWpyRq02 pic.twitter.com/vpnLPTRmLl

Newcastle United manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the new season, as they step up their preparations against Everton at Murrayfield this evening.

Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who have lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

Saturday’s match ended Fulham 1 Newcastle 1.

Ahead of each game we ask one of our writers to come up with three positives and three negatives following the game.

Plenty to talk about after this Fulham one…

A match that saw Newcastle United take the lead with a stunning long range Jacob Murphy left foot stunner.

Only for Fulham to deny United all three points only a couple of minutes after the restart.

On this occasion it is ‘Matt Busby said to Joe Harvey…’ with the positives and negatives:

I criticised Hornicek on Monday; it was deserved, after he let the ball squirm under him to gift Thierno Barry his goal.

Five days later at Craven Cottage, the young Czech is probably our MOTM, a string of decent saves from Oscar Bobb, Josh King, Timothy Castagne, before the pick of the lot, diving full stretch to deny Ryan Sessegnon in injury time and preserve United’s point.

Although it was very frustrating to concede less than three minutes after Jacob Murphy had put us ahead, we could have still conspired to lose this one, so a point is a point and after Monday’s debacle, we needed to limit our losses.

That’s four games in London this season; three wins and a draw with only one goal conceded.

That was a peach of a strike from Jacob Murphy in the 80th minute and it should have delivered us all three points.

Not only did he score that cracker, I thought Murphy was our best outfield player today, responsible for creating two big chances for Barnes and Burn, whose disallowed goal should have stood in my opinion.

Murphy also did some decent defensive work, tracking back in support of Dedic, so it’s a toss up between him and the keeper for my MOTM award.

Not only did our lead take less than three minutes to dismantle, it was the manner in which it was lost that was so annoying.

Unnecessary panicking, unable to clear our lines and an awful deflection all conspiring against us. We still look very brittle at the back.

I thought pairing these two in the centre of the park was a no-brainer and long overdue.

In some respects, I was a little surprised to see Matthias Jaissle agreeing with me today, but when the team was announced, the German had seemingly taken heed.

Unfortunately, neither was able to stamp their authority on the game and the so-called double pivot didn’t work out; Fulham dominated possession and our transition from defence into attack was very sluggish.

It wasn’t a surprise that both were replaced but I don’t think Jaissle should give up on this pairing based solely on today.

He may well be, although he wasn’t at fault for their equaliser, just like he can’t be blamed for what looks like such poor recruitment over the past couple of windows.

What concerns me about this manager is that he doesn’t seem capable of getting a tune out of his players and where is Aladji Bamba?

West Ham United will have to make do without one of their – ahem – key players when the Championship resumes after the international break. Following on from today’s 2-1 defeat against a modest Blackburn Rovers side who knew exactly what they were about this afternoon, the Hammers go into a two week period of ‘deep reflection’ before restarting against Preston North End in two weeks time.

And they’ll have to do so without £4 million – oops that should read £40 million man Maximilian Kilman who picked up a fifth yellow card of the campaign – this one apparently for simulation after being smacked cleanly in the head –  and he will therefore sit out the first game back after the merciful lull in West Ham’s shambolic descent from the top end  of the table..

In depressing echoes of a year ago, West Ham still have to set up repeatedly with Kilman and Mavropanos as the defensive pairing of doom – only a matter of time before one, or other of them is caught hopelessly out of position.

At least Dinos Mavropanos offers a goal threat – whilst when paired with Kilman is made to look defensively distinctly ordinary

In what can only be seen as a massive mistake, West Ham chose not to add to their centre back keystone cops double act in the summer window, letting Todibo leave on loan and therefore both committing and condemning themselves to the duo for the foreseeable future.

West Ham solved the problem last year – but not the number of points lost – by bringing in Axel Disasi in the January window and you’d expect them to make a similar move for an urgent upgrade this winter. Too little, too late, much as it was a year ago.

We can only hope that Airidas Golambeckis impresses enough in his outing alongside Dinos in two weeks’ time that he keeps Kilman out of the side.

To be honest, it is tough watching the same pairing year after year making the same mistakes and costing clean sheet after clean sheet. #2075. Celtic hero Ramon Vega on how Scotland can help him save football from Infantino

For the vast majority of people in Scotland, the name of Ramon Vega will chiefly evoke memories of his short but successful spell at the heart of a treble-winning Celtic defence in the early 2000s. But might they soon know him as the saviour of FIFA, and even – as is his aim – the saviour of football’s soul?

The man himself would like to think so. For over a decade, he has been painstakingly preparing and positioning himself for a run at the FIFA presidency, and now, with trust in the organisation arguably at an all-time low under the leadership of Gianni Infantino, he believes that his time has come.

If faith is to be restored in football as a sport - never mind FIFA as a governing body - after Infantino presided over the highest World Cup ticket prices in history and then attempted to sell a 20 per cent stake in a new commercial entity controlling the rights to FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup, to private investors without consulting the FIFA Council, he is firmly of the mind that Infantino has to resign.

As it stands, Infantino intends to seek another term as FIFA president in March next year, a prospect that is, for Vega, unthinkable.

“Speaking frankly, the trust is completely gone,” Vega said.

“You can’t go behind the council and try to sell privatisation. How can you even think that you could still sit there? In any public company, if you are a member or board member, never mind actually the chairman of the board, and you are behind the scenes selling the shares? A resignation on the next day is automatic.

“I am not sure where the council are with this, but that should be immediate resignation. From my point of view, if he had any balls and had some moral and ethical understanding what the damage is here, he should come out and put his hands up and say sorry.

“Mistakes? I don't believe in mistakes at this level. This was not a mistake. This was on purpose. Mistakes you can do potentially in another way, but we are talking here one of the biggest selloffs ever in world football and one of the biggest assets of world football. That is something where you can't make mistakes. It is impossible. I don't accept mistakes in this case.

“This is completely delusional mismanagement how that has been handled and by default the resignation should be done. But it is not going to happen, because we know the man we are dealing with here.”

For Vega’s campaign to succeed, he has many hurdles yet to clear. To that end, he confirmed that he has already reached out to the Scottish FA about supporting his candidacy as he attempts to secure the five nominations required to make the ballot.

“First of all, I have a great relationship with Scottish football anyway because I played there. I have a natural affinity with it through Celtic. It's a natural kind of forum to talk.

“I am going to speak to the SFA and I hope the Scots and SFA now also understand from where I'm coming from in their mind as well and support. I think I can help them quite a lot, and not from an intimidation way.

“Scottish football has an important part within FIFA because it's one of the foundations of the invention of football with England, as well the oldest rules of the game. So, that's very important and I'm very proud that I actually played in that country as well.

“For me, it would be absolutely enormous pleasure that they support me in going forward.”

In positioning himself almost as the anti-Infantino, it may be helpful to also know a little about the man we are dealing with on the other side of this coin outside of his brief love affair with Celtic.

After retiring from the professional game, the former Tottenham Hotspur, Watford and Switzerland defender carved out a career in international finance, and has since advised football clubs on finance, commercial growth, strategy and football development.

He first explored running for the FIFA presidency in 2015 and made subsequent efforts in 2019 and 2022, without ultimately making the ballot. His last campaign ended under what he describes as ‘difficult and deeply questionable circumstances’.

Undeterred, Vega, alongside his wife Claudia, who has an extensive background at the highest level of the professional game herself in technical and operational roles, has produced an 11-page document outlining why the time is now right for him to pick up that fight once more.

At its heart is a sense that football – the fans, the players and the many other stakeholders – are desperate for change; that there is a hunger for a different type of leadership, where supporters are the priority, and not simply treated as customers.

While not naïve to the political machinations of an organisation on the scale of FIFA, he is also an unashamed romantic about the power of football to inspire, and it is the disillusionment of fans and their potential disconnection from the game that is his greatest fear.

“I played the game at the highest level, I served the game at the highest level. I have been giving to the game everything possible for where I am today. If I look back now, without the game, I couldn't talk now today with you regarding the game going forward or potentially lead the future of that game.

“I think it was important to put such a document together because people need to understand where this all comes from. It is coming with an enormous experience behind the scenes. People will see these guys are not coming in, and even though we are not inside the system, we understand the system extremely well. It was a lot of work from my wife as well because she understands the industry.

“If you think of the ticket prices for the World Cup as an example, I find this insane. The people's game, the game I played since I was a little boy, the one at an early stage I had access to for a small amount of money, which inspired me to go into football.

“When you start to minimise or even limit access because you start to be an elite game just to squeeze another pound, then you’re doing something completely wrong. You are not creating legacy or growth, inspiring the next generation.

“Let’s say you are a father, you’ve got two kids, they love football. Then there is a huge World Cup coming up, and you’re spending five to ten grand because you’re going to do as a father everything to show your kids the best of the best, which is the World Cup. But a father has to take out a mortgage or is taking credit and paying off for the next three to five years? That is not fair.

“And then you are also limiting because not everybody can afford this. Most football fans are not coming from a champagne background. They are the soul and I love them because they have really the proper passion.

“When I was at Celtic that was one of the best periods of time and one of the best set of fans on the planet because they’re coming with passion; they do everything for that club.

“We need to make sure that these fans leave also a legacy for their kids and the kids of their kids. But if you stop them because it is too expensive, you’re completely missing the whole inspiration of the young generation to play football in the future.

“You can see the society is ready for change. That's what we want. The fans have been neglected massively. They have been used as a customer. They are not customers; they are loyal fans and they have to be respected.”

As Vega wryly notes, though, it isn’t always a commitment towards the betterment of football or advancing the interests of the rank-and-file fan that gains the support of member federations, but the distribution of cold, hard cash.

He finds it staggering that FIFA now holds a reserve of $6bn and believes the distribution of FIFA funds has effectively become a form of political currency. His proposal is that more than 90 per cent of money coming into FIFA should be distributed to its member associations rather than accumulating within the organisation.

“There is no doubt that this way of being afraid to speak out, because they have certain commitments already done, shouldn't really happen,” he said.

“At the end of the day, it is the interest of the game and not the interest of a personal achievement. If you start to doubt the integrity or your moral or ethical side, then you have to ask yourself in the mirror: do I really do something to serve this game, or am I part of all of them in this gang?

“I think it is important now that people understand that can’t be happening anymore. They are still afraid because we went through it with lots of other federations. This is why it makes me angry because you don't develop the football side; it is more political currency that comes into place.

“Once the political currency is involved, then it is a wrong path. We are not going in the right direction.

“Let me just be very clear. Any money that comes into FIFA belongs to the associations. There are certain accountabilities in terms of how you manage that money. But in my view, 90 percent plus of that money has to be distributed immediately to all these associations with certain check balances and accountability.

“Holding back that kind of level of reserves when I see some of the smaller African or Asian federations, where they are struggling to have under 15s, under 16s traveling to another friendly game because the costs are so high. This is what you guys potentially need to explain as well in the UK or in Europe. If you withhold the money for these people, you’re stopping the development.

“That is one thing that definitely needs to be changed and not to be using it as a currency. At the moment, I feel it. You do something for me and I’m going to distribute that money. Like now, he [Infantino] says, 'I am going to send you all 25 million dollars.' But he isn't sending anything; that is their money. You are not doing anything else better than giving back what is their money.

“Why is that not yet distributed and why was this not mentioned at the Vancouver Congress? That's the question - why is that mentioned only now when the topic [of the sell-off] comes into it. Because of intimidation, and the fear of standing up for something that is right.

“We need to come back to a democratic way of standing up. Either you can agree or disagree, that's the way that democracy works. But you can't have an autocratic way of dealing with this. It is impossible.”

It is safe to say, then, that under Vega’s watch, spectacles such as the awarding of the FIFA Peace Prize to Donald Trump, or a national leader personally lobbying the FIFA president over a disciplinary case involving his country's team, would be a thing of the past.

Trump, infamously, personally asked Infantino to review USA striker Folarin Balogun's red card during the World Cup before the implementation of the forward's automatic one-match suspension was controversially suspended.

“Well, this is what happens when you’re cosying up with these people,” he said.

“I understand that it is the host nation. I have been in the game for a long time as well and I understand the politics, but you don't cosy up. You are friendly, you respect them, but there is a distance from the politics.

“Yes, I respect the host, I respect they put money into the hosting it. That's where it stays. Why do we need to have a peace award? I wouldn’t do that at all. That's not my responsibility, it is not my mandate. My mandate is to make sure the game is run properly with integrity and the distribution of the money goes to the right associations, and to make sure the grassroots has the right infrastructure to grow. That's my mandate.

“Giving a peace award? Not my mandate. That's for the Nobel Prize committee. They are an institution that has been doing this for years; they are responsible, they are respectable within the industry. That's not a matter of FIFA.

“It is the same thing when people are calling you up, 'Listen, I’d rather they do this.' That's the very question; I would say it is not my duty. I'm not answering them with, ‘I'm going to look into it’, like a partner in crime.

“I understand the motion from the American point of view. They want to make sure their country gets the best.

“But as a FIFA president, you have to tell them, 'Listen, it is not my responsibility. I'm sorry, I can't help you.' And you leave it there. That's it. That should have been a five-second discussion.”

Vega remains remarkably clued up about goings-on in Scottish football, particularly, and perhaps predictably, the fortunes of his former manager Martin O'Neill, who he was pleasantly surprised to see pulling on the old tracksuit once more.

“He’s still got it. I sent him a message when he took over again. We have always had a good rapport.

“Everyone knows he’s a legend. He’s done an unbelievable job for that club. In the twenty-first century, I would say he’s the best manager Celtic had in terms of achievements and from where he took Celtic. After nine years of Rangers’ domination, he came and won the treble straight away. It’s remarkable.

“This is what sport is all about, the legacy you leave behind, and not the money. Legacy is more important to be remembered by.

"At that age, I think it’s refreshing for someone to take over that job. Once you have that management style, it never goes away. You just have to adapt to the new football world and how the youngster’s mentality is different to 20 or 30 years ago. That’s the only difference between coaches from twenty years ago and now, it’s adapting to the new world we are living in.

“Sometimes it’s good to have that conservative past as I still think that works best with a balance."

By reframing the role of FIFA president as one of service to the game rather than the accumulation of personal power or wealth, Vega hopes he will win over many beyond these borders too, who have become disillusioned with the way the game is presently run.

“Not the individual person. That's very important to understand and that's the way I want to have it. We need to go back to a democratic way of decisions and accountability of the organisation.

“I think the president is there to make sure he is an ambassador, make sure that it is running properly. It doesn't mean he is the dictator or the autocratic way of dealing in it. He has to have consensus within all the member associations, the council. Respect, not like the disrespect now and the betrayal.

“That [the attempted sell-off] was betrayal. I don't know how these guys can still shake the hands of such a person who would betray them like that. Because that's really a betrayal from my point of view.

“So, it's important to make it not autocratic anymore, make it democratic. Put a formula in place and certain accountability and check balances. Certain power to be limited to a certain level because you still need to have certain authority to do it. That's what it is. But in a democratic way.

“It is one of the first things we need to look to in the first 100 days. I am inviting all the stakeholders to the table to put the consensus together how they view things, how we view things, how we’re going to change that. So, everybody is responsible too because in the end, the organisation belongs to the associations. That has to be very clear. It belongs to the association, not to me. Absolutely.

“It's very important that the guy who is running FIFA now knows it.”

#2074. ‘For Newcastle United it was like a final’ Alvaro Arbeloa

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Alvaro Arbeloa watched on as Fulham went behind to a Jacob Murphy wonder strike with ten minutes of normal tie remaining.

Once the game restarted though, the home side swiftly equalising.

A smart finish from Muniz but helped by a deflection in the build up and then another when his shot beat Hornicek.

That giving Fulham a point, though Newcastle United had edged the game.

Alvaro Arbeloa speaking to BBC Sport: “You always want to win, especially at home. We knew how difficult it was going to be against Newcastle United and you could feel from the start that, for them, it was like a final. They were very, very aggressive. They are a very physical team, they were marking us man-to-man. I think we did a very good first half, we controlled the game, had very good chances but the second half was more open, chances for both teams.”

Alvaro Arbeloa on Jacob Murphy’s long range left foot stunner: “It is unbelievable because we concede another amazing goal from outside the box, with the left foot… it’s incredible. But we responded really, really well and could draw the game and have another good chance with Ryan Sessegnon. It’s another point, we wanted to win the game but it is what it is and we need to continue working hard.”

#2073. Motherwell ace feeling 21 again as he embraces senior role

Motherwell striker Callum Hendry aims to be a key player on and off the park after getting back to fitness.

Hendry made his first appearance of the season in Saturday’s 1-0 win over St Mirren following knee surgery, having come back from a four-month lay-off in April last season.

Speaking ahead of Saturday’s trip to face Dundee United, the former St Johnstone player said: “I sorted out the double hernia and then playing and training consistently probably covered the injury that I had.

“At the start of summer I started running again and I had really bad, really angry tendonitis, so it just needed fixing. I got the operation and I feel good now and hopefully I can put it behind me.

“I’m very optimistic. The more minutes I get, the fitter I’ll get, the sharper I’ll get. And I’ve seen that the team’s creating a lot of chances.”

Hendry, Paul McGinn and Oscar Priestman all returned off the bench against Saints to give the squad a lift.

“I’ve actually felt like there’s a bit of a glow around training having us back, because it’s such a tight-knit group,” the 28-year-old said. “It was just nice for us all to come back for the same game, and win it.

“The culture hasn’t changed, which I think is important, because we created such a good culture last year and we’ve kept it somehow, which is quite rare for such an overhaul of players.

“There’s a few younger lads in there, different changing room really, but still got the same feel to it. The boys are still close.

“It’s important that you stick together. They have had to stick together through some tough results the last couple of months where they haven’t really deserved them.

“I’ve had a few boys speak to me and ask me for advice, more this time than the last few seasons.

“I still feel 21, but my body tells me different sometimes. But it’s nice to be that guy because I always leaned on the older pros when I was younger.”

#2072. Sky Germany: Krösche heading for Milan but compensation must be discussed – the situation

Sources in Germany are confirming that Markus Krösche should be announced by AC Milan in the coming weeks, ready to start in January.

It is seemingly not a very well-kept secret by this point that Milan are looking to appoint Krösche as their new Head of Football, having made an attempt to get him in the summer. Sources in Italy have claimed things are done, but their German colleagues have always been a bit more hesitant.

Now, Sky Germany confirm that Krösche’s future likely lies in Italy because a move to Milan is becoming increasingly likely. However, no deal has been finalised yet: officials from both clubs still need to hold talks as Krösche is only on leave from Frankfurt.

His contract, which runs until 2028, is currently still valid. The 46-year-old insisted on having a release clause included in his contract. Specifically, this means that any club wanting to hire him before the summer of 2027 will have to pay a fee of approximately €5-7m, or negotiate with Eintracht.

No advanced talks have yet taken place, but Sky do add that Krösche is expected to take on the role of Head of Football with Milan. A start date of January 1, 2027 – coinciding with the start of the winter transfer window – is being discussed.

Meanwhile, Eintracht Frankfurt have already settled the question of Krösche’s successor. Joti Chatzialexiou is coming from 1. FC Nürnberg and will take over the position of sporting director. So, it seems like just a matter of time.

#2069. Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG

Unai Emery’s Aston Villa 2.0 remain under construction but from the wreckage of a difficult summer there has emerged a potential star for the future.

Emery may have now suffered four successive defeats in the Super Cup, yet the big positive from a balmy night in Salzburg was the performance of teenage forward Brian Madjo. Aged 17 years and 212 days, Madjo became the youngest player to start and score in this continental showpiece, just over a week after he was given permission to play for his club.

Signed from Metz for £10m in January, Madjo had been prevented from playing because of Fifa’s rules on the international transfer of minors. Villa’s appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport to have him registered was upheld on August 4 and what a prospect he appears.

Born in Enfield but raised in Luxembourg, there has been a huge buzz around him since his arrival in the new year.

Paris St-Germain have produced an abundance of talented teenagers over the years and Madjo did not look out of place here.Désiré Doué’s second-half strike secured PSG the Super Cup – contested by the winners of the Champions League and Europa League – for the second successive year, but Emery will have seen enough to give him renewed confidence.

Desire Doue puts PSG 2-1 ahead despite originally being flagged offside 🫣📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vnMIZCWJaj

His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Hemmings, 19, has emerged from the academy and already made a real impression on his manager. Despite the high regard for those youngsters, this always appeared likely to be a tough proposition against a full-strength PSG team. Indeed, before this game in Salzburg only 39 per cent of Europa League winners have beaten their Champions League rivals in this fixture.

The French champions did start slowly, but had been cranking up the pressure before taking a 20th minute lead with a spectacular strike from their Georgian superstar.

Doué forced a save from Marco Bizot and, after Villa failed to clear, the loose ball landed in the path of Kvaratskhelia, who cut inside on the left to his right foot before smashing a shot into the roof of the net.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia puts PSG 1-0 ahead vs Aston Villa 🔥📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/BIf8njpaSx

It was a strike of sheer power and accuracy, catching Bizot by surprise. PSG briefly appeared in control, but Villa responded superbly. In 17 minutes they created six goal-scoring chances before the outstanding Madjo finally made one of them count.

Before his goal, he had narrowly missed the target twice with a pair of headers from John McGinn’s crosses. Villa also had another opportunity 10 minutes before half-time, when Pacho’s mistake allowed Hemmings to run from the centre circle unopposed. As he entered the penalty area, the PSG defenders had raced back to recover and a promising moment ended with Madjo curling a shot wide.

Brian Madjo with a big chance to put Aston Villa level 😮📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pqsC5Hor15

PSG goalkeeper Matvey Safonov then produced his first save just before the break, turning away Boubacar Kamara’s close-range header. Villa did carve out another golden chance when Madjo’s strength took hm past Pacho, but he hit the outside of the post. Madjo’s moment did come, though, as he once again bullied Pacho to divert a McGinn cross into the roof of the net.

Brian Madjo at 17-years-old scores in the UEFA Super Cup Final 🤯📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/PccX7FxjAr

Villa were buoyant, but it was PSG who scored the crucial second goal after Doué was awarded the goal following a VAR review. Doué was sent clear down the right by substitute Ousmane Dembélé and confidently beat Bizot, with reviews concluding that he had been played onside by Matty Cash.

The game was refereed by Omar Artan, the Somali referee who was supposed to officiate at the World Cup but was denied entry to the United States.

It became rather fractious as time began to tick away, with McGinn booked after complaining over the placement of a free-kick. Madjo was replaced by Tammy Abraham with 17 minutes left and this will be an evening he will never forget.

PSG (4-3-3): Safonov, Hakimi, Marquinhos, Pacho, Mendes (Hernandez 75), Neves (Ruiz 75), Vitinha, Emery, Akliouche, (Dembele 45), Doue (Mayulu 87), Kvaratskhelia (Buraldo 88).Substitutes: Chevalier (g), Zabarnyi, Digne, Fernandez, Barcola, Ndjantou, Mbaye.Villa (4-2-3-1): Bizot, Cash, Lindelof, Torres (Mings 80), Maatsen, Kamara (Bogarde 72), Gomes (Barkley 79), McGinn 7 (Alysson 73), Buendia, Hemmings, Madjo (Abraham 72).Substitutes: Wright (g), Asemota (g), Barkley, Nedeljkovic, Cisse, Rowe, Burrowes, Lynch.Booked: Gomes, Torres, McGinn.Referee: Omar Artan (Somalia).

After the officials and the Aston Villa players receive their medals, it is time for the 2026 Uefa Super Cup winners PSG to receive their medals. The last man up is their captain Marquinhos, who has won a staggering 40 trophies during his time at PSG. He takes the trophy from Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin and lifts it above his head alongside his teammates.

PSG are your 2026 UEFA Super Cup Champions 🏆📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/1qCKEQ0IPK

Both Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have been heavily linked with moves to Liverpool this summer and neither player came off the bench for PSG tonight. Does that indicate that potentially those moves could be close, with neither played risked of picking up an injury?

Luis Enrique has now won 13 trophies with PSG. Serial winner 🏆 pic.twitter.com/RAsyI1Ui2s

💬 "We are ALWAYS hungry you know... we want more, we want more" Désiré Doué reflects on PSG's UEFA Super Cup Final win.📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nwreU1Skz7

Aston Villa will take on Borussia Mönchengladbach on Saturday in their final game of pre-season before they take on Brighton on the south coast on the opening weekend of the new Premier League season.

PSG play Lens in the Trophée des Champions on Sunday before they kick off the defence of their Ligue 1 crown at home against Rennes.

Possession: PSG 61%- Aston Villa 39%Shots: 12-15Shots on target: 6-4Corners: 0-2Touches in opposition box: 29-34

Buendia has a late chance to equalise for Aston Villa from Maatsen’s cross but his header goes wide.

Not long after, the final whistle goes and PSG win the Super Cup for the second straight year. Last year they beat Tottenham on penalties, this time they beat Aston Villa 2-1. Unai Emery’s side acquitted themselves well and will regret some of their missed chances tonight. An entertaining affair in Salzburg.

PSG win back-to-back UEFA Super Cup's following goals from Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue 🏆📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vzMx6rGjuo

Dembele feeds a pass into the Villa box looking to pick out the run of Hakimi but there is slightly too much on it and Bizot is out to gather.

Into the final minute of added time we go.

Aston Villa are running out of time to find a late equaliser.

Maatsen brings Dembele down not far outside the Aston Villa box but play goes on as the latter gets up and shoots, with his effort saved by Bizot.

One final change for PSG as their other goalscorer tonight, Kvaratskhelia, is replaced by Beraldo. A defender comes on for an attacker as Luis Enrique’s side look to hold on for the victory.

Mayulu is coming on for Doue, whose goal may well have won back-to-back Super Cups for PSG.

The ball falls to Kvaratskhelia on the right side of the box and the Georgian chips it over Bizot but Cash is on hand to clear. Aston Villa then counter and Abraham feeds a pass forward at the perfect time to pick out the run of Alysson into the PSG box. Alysson then plays it across the six-yard box but neither Abraham nor Maatsen are there to meet the cross.

Double change for Aston Villa as Barkley and Mings replace Gomes and Torres, who were both on yellow cards.

Alysson, only just on the pitch, does brilliantly down Aston Villa’s right and drives into the PSG penalty area. His cross is parried away by Safonov straight into the path of Gomes, whose shot is blocked by Zaire-Emery.

PSG are making a double substitution as Ruiz and L Hernandez come on. Neves and Mendes, who had been struggling with cramp, go off.

Aston Villa are going to make a triple change as Abraham, Alysson and Bogarde come on. 17-year-old Madjo is one of those to be replaced as is McGinn, who has been booked as he goes off. The Aston Villa captain is distinctly unimpressed with the officials.

The space opens up for Mendes to take on the shot from range and he obliges, forcing Bizot into a decent save. Kvaratskhelia is unable to make contact with the follow-up. Mendes seems to be struggling with some cramp.

We are nearly 70 minutes into the game but Unai Emery has still not turned to his bench yet.

Aston Villa have an immediate chance to equalise through Hemmings but the 19-year-old’s effort from inside the box is straight at Safonov. That was a big chance for Hemmings.

Down the other end, Gomes is booked for a challenge from behind on Doue.

The VAR has checked it and there was no offside so the original decision is overturned and the goal is given. Doue is played in behind by Dembele down the right channel and is played onside by Cash on the far side. Doue takes it into the Villa penalty area and gets it onto his left foot. He curls it past Bizot and into the far corner.

Desire Doue puts PSG 2-1 ahead despite originally being flagged offside 🫣📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vnMIZCWJaj

Doue has the ball in the Aston Villa net but the offside flag has gone up. However, has Cash played Doue onside?

Cash’s cross from the right picks out Buendia at the front post but the latter’s header is off target. Unai Emery will be pretty happy with his side’s performance through the hour mark.

Mendes is a touch fortunate not to be penalised for a foul on McGinn as the Aston Villa captain spun the Portuguese defender on halfway. The referee must have thought both players had a hold of each other but I would lean towards Mendes probably fouling McGinn.

Other than 10/15 minutes in and around Kvaratskhelia’s goal, Aston Villa have put in a good performance and have created more chances than PSG. If anything, it will be Villa who will be disappointed that they have not scored more than once.

Just inside the PSG penalty area, McGinn cuts onto his left to get his shot away and his deflected effort is saved by Safonov diving to his right.

One of Aston Villa’s coaches has been booked for some protestations after Torres is penalised for a foul on Doue. Torres is also booked for that challenge.

Two of Aston Villa’s best players tonight thus far have been teenagers; 19-year-old Hemmings and 17-year-old Madjo. Aston Villa have seen some key, senior players depart this summer but will take joy from the performances of this pair.

Luis Enrique has decided he needed to make a change at the break as Dembele replaces Akliouche, who was quiet on his official debut for PSG after his move from Monaco.

Incredible to think he is only 17 years and 212 days old. He’s been all over PSG centre-back Willian Pacho and thoroughly deserves his goal.

The teenager could even have had a hat-trick. What a second-half this could be.

Madjo has managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s Georgian magician Kvicha Kvaratskhelia, which is quite some achievement.

Possession: PSG 67%-33% Aston VillaShots: 6-10Shots on target: 2-2Corners: 0-2Touches in opposition box: 11-17

After one added minute, the first half is brought to an end and we are all square at 1-1 in Salzburg. Kvaratskhelia had put PSG in front but Madjo’s goal on the stroke of half-time has Aston Villa level at the break.

On the stroke of half-time, the 17-year-old levels for Aston Villa and finally takes his fourth big chance of the night. It is perhaps the hardest chance he has had as McGinn’s cross comes all the way to the back post. Madjo is being held by Pacho but somehow gets his foot to it and his shot goes into the roof of the net. What a moment for the 17-year-old!

Brian Madjo at 17-years-old scores in the UEFA Super Cup Final 🤯📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/PccX7FxjAr

Madjo has his third massive chance of this first half and this shot comes off the post. Buendia feeds a pass forward into the path of Madjo, who appeared to be blocked by Pacho but he outmuscles him. Madjo then fires towards goal but it strikes the outside of the post. In a parallel universe, Madjo could have ahd a first-half hat-trick.

Aston Villa have had a few great chances in this first half and there is another. A free-kick into the PSG penalty area causes issues for the French side and Kamara’s header towards goal is saved by Safonov.

Madjo has his second huge chance of this first half. Once more it is McGinn who provides the cross. The Scot does really well on the right side of the box to fake the cross with his left and instead delivers with his right. He picks out Madjo at the back post and the 17-year-old should score but his header misses the target. What a story it would have been had the 17-year-old scored two goals against the Champions League winners.

Aston Villa have just settled things down. Either side of Kvaratskhelia’s goal, they were on the ropes but have calmed things down.

Hemmings is played in and he could potentially have gone down twice under challenges from Hakimi and then Mendes. The ball then falls to 17-year-old Madjo on the left side of the box. He opens up his body and tries to curl into the far corner but his effort goes wide.

Referees are now hot on players taking too long over throw-ins, with Mendes falling foul of that. That is one of the fairly new rules that will be good for the game.

A huge chance for 17-year-old Madjo to equalise. McGinn picks out the young striker with a sublime cross from the right. Madjo is just eight yards out and has a free header but it goes just wide of the far post. Aston Villa should be level.

Brian Madjo with a big chance to put Aston Villa level 😮📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pqsC5Hor15

After Aston Villa had made a solid start to this game, it is all PSG right now and Villa are on the ropes at the moment. PSG work it beautifully down their left after a sublime one-two between Mendes and Kvaratskhelia. Mendes drives down the left wing and has a cross into the box first-time which he declines. The Portuguese defender then has four different teammates that he could pick out in the penalty area but his cross misses all four.

PSG want a penalty. Kvaratskhelia shows great feet out on the left to drive into the Aston Villa penalty area. Gomes is on his back and Kvaratskhelia goes down. It did look like he was always looking to go down and it would have been very soft.

A few minutes after I said that Aston Villa had done a decent job of keeping PSG at bay, Luis Enrique’s side take the lead. Bizot had just made a great reflex save to deny Doue but he is unable to stop Kvaratskhelia’s effort. The Georgian cuts inside onto his right just inside the Aston Villa penalty area and gets his shot away quickly after quick feet. There is great venom on the shot and it beats Bizot, who thought Kvaratskhelia was going to go for the far corner but instead hit it at the near post. Could Bizot have saved that? Perhaps but Kvaratskhelia did belt that shot.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia puts PSG 1-0 ahead vs Aston Villa 🔥📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/BIf8njpaSx

As you would expect, PSG are dominating possession but thus far have been unable to create any genuine chances, much to Aston Villa’s credit. But, with the players PSG have at their disposal, they can cause chaos in a moment.

Tensions just start to simmer. McGinn gives a foul away on Mendes, who then attempts to take the free-kick a good few yards further forward from where it was. McGinn repeatedly tries to stop Mendes from taking it further forward before the referee steps in to end the dispute.

Moments later, Kamara decides to shoot from range and his low, driving effort goes wide of Safonov’s right post. With Onana injured long-term and Tielemans now at Manchester United, Kamara’s importance to Aston Villa is even higher.

In last year’s Super Cup, PSG were stunned in the first hour against Tottenham as went 2-0 down before coming back to win on penalties. PSG have played fewer friendlies than Aston Villa up until this point so there may be a little more rustiness in Luis Enrique’s side than Unai Emery’s.

This is going to be a very tall order for Aston Villa, who look very different tonight to how they ended last season, up against a team of PSG’s calibre. Not only have Villa sold some key players like Rogers and Tielemans but the likes of Konsa and Watkins are yet to return after the World Cup.

McGinn is afforded too much space and time to cut onto his left foot out on the right and whip a dangerous cross towards the far post. Pacho is on hand to head away with a great defensive header.

Moments later, good work from Maatsen out on the left earns Aston Villa a corner. Unai Emery’s side have made a decent start to this game. Buendia’s delivery into the near post is headed away by Marquinhos.

We are under way in Salzburg, where it has been a very hot day but the temperature has cooled a touch with the sun having set in Austria.

Some huge banners are on display on the pitch, displaying not only the emblems of the two clubs but also images of the trophy lifts that have earned these sides a place in tonight’s game. Both sides emerge from the tunnel, past the trophies they won with the two captains carrying them out, and we are moments away from kick-off in Salzburg. What will we learn from the “new Aston Villa” tonight? After the sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, this is a Villa team in transition.

Unai Emery virtually admitted last night it could be another slow start to the season, like last year. Villa face a full-strength PSG team hoping to win the Super Cup for the second time in a row.

I don’t think we can take much from this result tonight, whatever it is. Villa cannot be properly judged until the window closes. Don’t bother telling that to Unai Emery, though. He is ready to continue defying the doubters.

The Champions League and Europa League winners fight it out in the Uefa Super Cup in Salzburg as PSG take on Aston Villa. PSG took on English opposition in the Super Cup a year ago, when they played Tottenham. PSG fell 2-0 down in that game in Udine but scored two late goals to take it to penalties, where they won 4-3. These sides met in the Champions League knockout stages two seasons ago; PSG did progress from the quarter-final encounter as they went on to win the competition but not without a scare as Aston Villa did win at Villa Park and PSG only progressed 5-4 on aggregate. The two clubs have been involved in a transfer this week, with left-back Lucas Digne re-joining PSG from Aston Villa.

Aston Villa have played in the Super Cup once before back in 1982 when they took in Barcelona. They lost the first leg 1-0 over at Camp Nou but fought back to win the second leg 3-0 at Villa Park to claim the trophy. Aston Villa were last in action out in the Far East last Friday, falling to a 2-1 defeat to Bayern Munich in Hong Kong. It has been a big summer of change at the club, with key starters like Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans departing and the likes of Alejandro Garnacho and Joao Gomes arriving.

“I feel like the club is in a new era, with this possibility to fight for trophies,” Unai Emery told Uefa. “We are trying to be successful through, firstly, [building] a winning team, and then aiming for the positive consequences after it; winning trophies. To play the UEFA Super Cup is another opportunity to be there, the opportunity to win a trophy, to play against Paris Saint-Germain; the [best] team in the world now and another team we can compare [ourselves] with.”

Emery has confirmed that Ezri Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emiliano Martinez will not be involved as they are still on their breaks following the World Cup.

PSG have now won back-to-back Champions Leagues, beating Arsenal in the final last season. They have only played a couple of friendlies in pre-season, losing 3-0 to Mallorca before drawing 1-1 against Manchester United. Luis Enrique’s side will take on Lens in the Trophée des Champions on Sunday before kicking off the defence of their Ligue 1 title at home to Rennes.

“I focus on renewing that desire to win again,” Enrique told Uefa. “It is difficult to keep winning. Right now, we have a unique challenge; something that is practically unprecedented in the history of European football, which is to draw level with Real Madrid if we can win a third consecutive Champions League. No-one in history has won three in a row, only Real Madrid. We can equal them. But I do not think there is any team in Europe more motivated than us.

“No-one rules out PSG any more. Two years ago, it was impossible to put us among the favourites; not impossible, but we were not one of the favourites. Now, no one would say that Paris Saint-Germain are not the favourites. That is something we have earned, but if we are going to maintain that position, we have to work even harder.”

PSG have added Monaco winger Maghnes Akliouche and Digne to their ranks this summer. They are also pushing to sign Ferran Torres from Barcelona and Mika Godts from Ajax. Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have both been linked with moves to Liverpool but have been included in their squad for tonight’s game, as have Akliouche and Digne.

AC Milan owner Gerry Cardinale is ready to do what is possible to strengthen the squad when the window reopens.

La Gazzetta dello Sport report that the Milan owner is passionate, so while he got emotional after the derby win against Inter, he was also worried following the defeat to Bologna and the limitations it exposed. So, he is ready to give Ruben Amorim a helping hand, but where?

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Amorim said that, with the squad reduced by injuries, it’s difficult to press hard and play the football he prefers. We didn’t see that in the derby, but that’s another story.

Koni De Winter and Strahinja Pavlovic are the defenders who could use a union representative: they always play, never rest, and almost never come out early. Mario Gila is the other starter, but then Fikayo Tomori and Matteo Gabbia – the natural back-ups – are injured.

That leaves Filippo Terracciano and Sankhoun Diawara, who are more uncertainties than guarantees at present. A signing will arrive and Sporting CP’s Gonçalo Inacio was the target in the summer. The asking price was €40m then, and the Rossoneri could offer it again.

Tresoldi has been a Milan fan since childhood and doesn’t hide it. Will there be any other surprises? A wing-back is possible if Amorim decides the left side needs more momentum, or Samuel Chukwueze finds some company  in the treatment room. A goalkeeper to give Lorenzo Torriani a loan chance is possible. With Cardinale, nothing can be ruled out.
